The "Hello, World!" program is used to illustrate a language's basic syntax. The syntax of the language BASIC (1964)
was intentionally limited to make the language easy to learn. For example, <color=#3366CC>variables</color> are not declared before being
used. Also, variables are automatically initialized to zero. Here is an example computer program, in Basic, to <color=#3366CC>average</color> a
list of numbers:
Once the mechanics of basic computer programming are learned, more sophisticated and powerful languages are
available to build large computer systems.
History
Improvements in <color=#3366CC>software development</color> are the result of improvements in <color=#3366CC>computer hardware</color>. At each stage in
hardware's history, the task of <color=#3366CC>computer programming</color> changed dramatically.
Analytical Engine
In 1837, <color=#3366CC>Jacquard's loom</color> inspired <color=#3366CC>Charles Babbage</color> to attempt to build the <color=#3366CC>Analytical Engine</color>. The names of the
components of the calculating device were borrowed from the textile industry. In the textile industry, yarn was brought
from the store to be milled. The device had a store which consisted of memory to hold 1,000 numbers of 50 decimal
digits each. Numbers from the store were transferred to the mill for processing. The engine was programmed using two
sets of perforated cards. One set directed the operation and the other set inputted the variables. However, the
thousands of cogged wheels and gears never fully worked together.
<color=#3366CC>Ada Lovelace</color> worked for Charles Babbage to create a description of the Analytical Engine (1843). The description
contained Note G which completely detailed a method for calculating Bernoulli numbers using the Analytical Engine.
This note is recognized by some historians as the world's first computer program.
Universal Turing machine
In 1936, <color=#3366CC>Alan Turing</color> introduced the <color=#3366CC>Universal Turing machine</color>, a theoretical device that can model every computation. It
is a <color=#3366CC>finite-state machine</color> that has an infinitely long read/write tape. The machine can move the tape back and forth,
changing its contents as it performs an <color=#3366CC>algorithm</color>. The machine starts in the initial state, goes through a sequence of
steps, and halts when it encounters the halt state. All present-day computers are Turing complete.
ENIAC
The <color=#3366CC>Electronic Numerical Integrator And Computer</color> (ENIAC) was built between July 1943 and Fall 1945. It was a Turing
complete, general-purpose computer that used 17,468 <color=#3366CC>vacuum tubes</color> to create the <color=#3366CC>circuits</color>. At its core, it was a series of
Pascalines wired together. Its 40 units weighed 30 tons, occupied 1,800 sqft, and consumed $650 per hour (<color=#3366CC>in 1940s</color>
<color=#3366CC>currency</color>) in electricity when idle. It had 20 <color=#3366CC>base-10</color> accumulators. Programming the ENIAC took up to two months.
Three function tables were on wheels and needed to be rolled to fixed function panels. Function tables were connected
to function panels by plugging heavy black cables into plugboards. Each function table had 728 rotating knobs.
Programming the ENIAC also involved setting some of the 3,000 switches. Debugging a program took a week. It ran
from 1947 until 1955 at Aberdeen Proving Ground, calculating hydrogen bomb parameters, predicting weather
patterns, and producing firing tables to aim artillery guns.
Stored-program computers
Instead of plugging in cords and turning switches, a <color=#3366CC>stored-program computer</color> loads its instructions into <color=#3366CC>memory</color> just
like it loads its data into memory. As a result, the computer could be programmed quickly and perform calculations at
very fast speeds. <color=#3366CC>Presper Eckert</color> and John Mauchly built the ENIAC. The two engineers introduced the stored-program
concept in a three-page memo dated February 1944. Later, in September 1944, <color=#3366CC>John von Neumann</color> began working on
the ENIAC project. On June 30, 1945, von Neumann published the First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC, which
equated the structures of the computer with the structures of the human brain. The design became known as the <color=#3366CC>von</color>
<color=#3366CC>Neumann architecture</color>. The architecture was simultaneously deployed in the constructions of the <color=#3366CC>EDVAC</color> and <color=#3366CC>EDSAC</color>
computers in 1949.
The IBM System/360 (1964) was a family of computers, each having the same <color=#3366CC>instruction set architecture</color>. The Model
20 was the smallest and least expensive. Customers could upgrade and retain the same <color=#3366CC>application software</color>. The
Model 195 was the most premium. Each System/360 model featured <color=#3366CC>multiprogramming</color>—having multiple <color=#3366CC>processes</color> in
<color=#3366CC>memory</color> at once. When one process was waiting for <color=#3366CC>input/output</color>, another could compute.
IBM planned for each model to be programmed using PL/I. A committee was formed that included <color=#3366CC>COBOL</color>, <color=#3366CC>FORTRAN</color>
and <color=#3366CC>ALGOL</color> programmers. The purpose was to develop a language that was comprehensive, easy to use, extendible,
and would replace COBOL and FORTRAN. The result was a large and complex language that took a long time to
<color=#3366CC>compile</color>.
Computers manufactured until the 1970s had front-panel switches for manual programming. The computer program
was written on paper for reference. An instruction was represented by a configuration of on/off settings. After setting the
configuration, an execute button was pressed. This process was then repeated. Computer programs also were
automatically inputted via paper tape, <color=#3366CC>punched cards</color> or magnetic-tape. After the medium was loaded, the starting
address was set via switches, and the execute button was pressed.
Very Large Scale Integration
A major milestone in software development was the invention of the <color=#3366CC>Very Large Scale Integration</color> (VLSI) circuit (1964).
Robert Noyce, co-founder of Fairchild Semiconductor (1957) and <color=#3366CC>Intel</color> (1968), achieved a technological improvement to
refine the production of <color=#3366CC>field-effect transistors</color> (1959). The goal is to alter the <color=#3366CC>electrical resistivity and conductivity</color> of a
semiconductor junction. First, naturally occurring <color=#3366CC>silicate minerals</color> are converted into polysilicon rods using the Siemens
process. The Czochralski process then converts the rods into a monocrystalline silicon, boule crystal. The <color=#3366CC>crystal</color> is
then thinly sliced to form a wafer substrate. The planar process of photolithography then integrates unipolar transistors,

<color=#3366CC>capacitors</color>, <color=#3366CC>diodes</color>, and <color=#3366CC>resistors</color> onto the wafer to build a matrix of <color=#3366CC>metal–oxide–semiconductor</color> (MOS) transistors. The
MOS transistor is the primary component in integrated circuit chips.
Originally, <color=#3366CC>integrated circuit</color> chips had their function set during manufacturing. During the 1960s, controlling the
electrical flow migrated to programming a matrix of <color=#3366CC>read-only memory</color> (ROM). The matrix resembled a two-dimensional
array of fuses. The process to embed instructions onto the matrix was to burn out the unneeded connections.
In 1969, Busicom, a Japanese calculator company, contracted with <color=#3366CC>Intel</color> to manufacture 12 integrated circuit chips,
each for a specific calculator function. Ted Hoff, the engineer tasked with the assignment, realized he could build one
chip that could execute computer programs to perform the 12 calculator functions. The resulting chip was called the
Intel 4004 <color=#3366CC>microprocessor</color>.
The terms microprocessor and <color=#3366CC>central processing unit</color> (CPU) are now used interchangeably. However, CPUs predate
microprocessors. For example, the IBM System/360 (1964) had a CPU made from circuit boards containing discrete
components on ceramic substrates.
x86 series
In 1978, the modern software development environment began when Intel upgraded the Intel 8080 to the Intel 8086.
Intel simplified the Intel 8086 to manufacture the cheaper Intel 8088. <color=#3366CC>IBM</color> embraced the Intel 8088 when they entered
the <color=#3366CC>personal computer</color> market (1981). As <color=#3366CC>consumer</color> demand for personal computers increased, so did Intel's
microprocessor development. The succession of development is known as the <color=#3366CC>x86 series</color>. The x86 assembly language
is a family of backward-compatible <color=#3366CC>machine instructions</color>. Machine instructions created in earlier microprocessors were
retained throughout microprocessor upgrades. This enabled consumers to purchase new computers without having to
purchase new <color=#3366CC>application software</color>. The major categories of instructions are:
• Memory instructions to set and access numbers and strings in <color=#3366CC>random-access memory</color>.
• Integer <color=#3366CC>arithmetic logic unit</color> (ALU) instructions to perform the primary arithmetic operations on <color=#3366CC>integers</color>.
• Floating point ALU instructions to perform the primary arithmetic operations on <color=#3366CC>real numbers</color>.
• Call stack instructions to push and pop words needed to allocate memory and interface with <color=#3366CC>functions</color>.
• Single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) instructions to increase speed when multiple processors are available to
perform the same <color=#3366CC>algorithm</color> on an <color=#3366CC>array of data</color>.
Changing programming environment
VLSI circuits enabled the <color=#3366CC>programming environment</color> to advance from a computer terminal (until the 1990s) to a
<color=#3366CC>graphical user interface</color> (GUI) computer. Computer terminals limited programmers to a single shell running in a
<color=#3366CC>command-line environment</color>. During the 1970s, full-screen source code editing became possible through a text-based
user interface. Regardless of the technology available, the goal is to program in a <color=#3366CC>programming language</color>.
Programming paradigms and languages
Programming language features exist to provide building blocks to be combined to express programming ideals.
Ideally, a programming language should:
• express ideas directly in the code.
• express independent ideas independently.
• express relationships among ideas directly in the code.
• combine ideas freely.
• combine ideas only where combinations make sense.
• express simple ideas simply.
The programming style of a programming language to provide these building blocks may be categorized into
<color=#3366CC>programming paradigms</color>. For example, different paradigms may differentiate:
• procedural languages, <color=#3366CC>functional languages</color>, and <color=#3366CC>logical languages</color>.
• different levels of <color=#3366CC>data abstraction</color>.
• different levels of class hierarchy.
• different levels of input <color=#3366CC>datatypes</color>, as in container types and generic programming.
Each of these programming styles has contributed to the synthesis of different programming languages.
A programming language is a set of keywords, symbols, identifiers, and rules by which programmers can communicate
instructions to the computer. They follow a set of rules called a <color=#3366CC>syntax</color>.
• Keywords are reserved words to form declarations and statements.
• Symbols are characters to form <color=#3366CC>operations</color>, assignments, <color=#3366CC>control flow</color>, and <color=#3366CC>delimiters</color>.
• Identifiers are words created by programmers to form constants, <color=#3366CC>variable names</color>, structure names, and <color=#3366CC>function</color>
<color=#3366CC>names</color>.
• Syntax Rules are defined in the <color=#3366CC>Backus–Naur form</color>.
Programming languages get their basis from <color=#3366CC>formal languages</color>. The purpose of defining a solution in terms of its formal
language is to generate an <color=#3366CC>algorithm</color> to solve the underlining problem. An algorithm is a sequence of simple
instructions that solve a problem.
Generations of programming language
The evolution of programming languages began when the <color=#3366CC>EDSAC</color> (1949) used the first <color=#3366CC>stored computer program</color> in its
<color=#3366CC>von Neumann architecture</color>. Programming the EDSAC was in the first generation of programming language.
• The first generation of programming language is <color=#3366CC>machine language</color>. Machine language requires the programmer to
enter instructions using instruction numbers called <color=#3366CC>machine code</color>. For example, the ADD operation on the PDP-11
has instruction number 24576.
• The second generation of programming language is <color=#3366CC>assembly language</color>. Assembly language allows the
programmer to use <color=#3366CC>mnemonic</color> <color=#3366CC>instructions</color> instead of remembering instruction numbers. An <color=#3366CC>assembler</color> translates
each assembly language mnemonic into its machine language number. For example, on the PDP-11, the operation
24576 can be referenced as ADD R0,R0 in the source code. The four basic arithmetic operations have assembly
instructions like ADD, SUB, MUL, and DIV. Assemblers also have instructions like DW (Define Word) to reserve
<color=#3366CC>memory</color> cells. Then the MOV instruction can copy <color=#3366CC>integers</color> between <color=#3366CC>registers</color> and those memory cells.
* The basic structure of an assembly language statement is a label, <color=#3366CC>operation</color>, operand, and comment. * Labels allow
the programmer to work with <color=#3366CC>variable names</color>. The assembler will later translate labels into physical memory addresses.
* Operations allow the programmer to work with mnemonics. * Operands tell the assembler which data the operation
will process. The assembler will later translate mnemonics and operands into instruction numbers. * Comments allow
the programmer to articulate a narrative because the instructions alone may be opaque to humans. The key
characteristic of an assembly language program is it forms a one-to-one mapping to its corresponding machine
language target.
• The third generation of programming language uses <color=#3366CC>compilers</color> and <color=#3366CC>interpreters</color> to execute computer programs. The
distinguishing feature of a third generation language is its independence from particular hardware. Early languages

include <color=#3366CC>FORTAN</color> (1958), <color=#3366CC>COBOL</color> (1959), <color=#3366CC>ALGOL</color> (1960), and <color=#3366CC>BASIC</color> (1964). In 1973, the <color=#3366CC>C programming</color>
<color=#3366CC>language</color> emerged as a <color=#3366CC>high-level language</color> that produced efficient machine language instructions. Whereas
third-generation languages historically generated many machine instructions for each statement, C has statements
that may generate a single machine instruction. Moreover, an optimizing compiler might overrule the programmer
and produce fewer machine instructions than statements. Today, an entire <color=#3366CC>paradigm</color> of languages fill the
<color=#3366CC>imperative</color>, third generation spectrum.
• The fourth generation of programming language emphasizes what output results are desired, rather than how
programming statements should be constructed. <color=#3366CC>Declarative languages</color> attempt to limit side effects and allow
programmers to write code with relatively few errors. One popular fourth generation language is called <color=#3366CC>Structured</color>
<color=#3366CC>Query Language</color> (SQL). <color=#3366CC>Database</color> developers no longer need to process each database record one at a time.
Also, a simple select statement can generate output records without having to understand how they are retrieved.
Imperative languages
Imperative languages specify a sequential <color=#3366CC>algorithm</color> using declarations, expressions, and statements:
• A declaration introduces a <color=#3366CC>variable</color> name to the computer program and assigns it to a <color=#3366CC>datatype</color> – for example: var
x: integer;
• An expression yields a value – for example: 2 + 2 yields 4
• A statement might assign an expression to a variable or use the value of a variable to alter the program's <color=#3366CC>control</color>
<color=#3366CC>flow</color> – for example: x:= 2 + 2; if x = 4 then do_something;
Fortran
<color=#3366CC>FORTRAN</color> (1958) was unveiled as "The IBM Mathematical FORmula TRANslating system". It was designed for
scientific calculations, without string handling facilities. Along with declarations, expressions, and statements, it
supported:
• <color=#3366CC>arrays</color>.
• <color=#3366CC>subroutines</color>.
• "do" loops.
It succeeded because:
• programming and debugging costs were below computer running costs.
• it was supported by IBM.
• applications at the time were scientific.
However, non-IBM vendors also wrote Fortran compilers, but with a syntax that would likely fail IBM's compiler. The
American National Standards Institute (ANSI) developed the first Fortran standard in 1966. In 1978, Fortran 77 became
the standard until 1991. Fortran 90 supports:
• records.
• <color=#3366CC>pointers</color> to arrays.
COBOL
<color=#3366CC>COBOL</color> (1959) stands for "COmmon Business Oriented Language". Fortran manipulated symbols. It was soon realized
that symbols did not need to be numbers, so strings were introduced. The <color=#3366CC>US Department of Defense</color> influenced
COBOL's development, with <color=#3366CC>Grace Hopper</color> being a major contributor. The statements were English-like and verbose.
The goal was to design a language so managers could read the programs. However, the lack of structured statements
hindered this goal.
COBOL's development was tightly controlled, so dialects did not emerge to require ANSI standards. As a consequence,
it was not changed for 15 years until 1974. The 1990s version did make consequential changes, like <color=#3366CC>object-oriented</color>
<color=#3366CC>programming</color>.
Algol
<color=#3366CC>ALGOL</color> (1960) stands for "ALGOrithmic Language". It had a profound influence on programming language design.
Emerging from a committee of European and American programming language experts, it used standard <color=#3366CC>mathematical</color>
<color=#3366CC>notation</color> and had a readable, structured design. Algol was first to define its syntax using the <color=#3366CC>Backus–Naur form</color>. This
led to syntax-directed compilers. It added features like:
• block structure, where variables were local to their block.
• arrays with variable bounds.
• "for" loops.
• <color=#3366CC>functions</color>.
• <color=#3366CC>recursion</color>.
Algol's direct descendants include <color=#3366CC>Pascal</color>, Modula-2, <color=#3366CC>Ada</color>, Delphi and Oberon on one branch. On another branch the
descendants include <color=#3366CC>C</color>, <color=#3366CC>C++</color> and <color=#3366CC>Java</color>.
Basic
<color=#3366CC>BASIC</color> (1964) stands for "Beginner's All-Purpose Symbolic Instruction Code". It was developed at <color=#3366CC>Dartmouth College</color>
for all of their students to learn. If a student did not go on to a more powerful language, the student would still
remember Basic. A Basic interpreter was installed in the <color=#3366CC>microcomputers</color> manufactured in the late 1970s. As the
microcomputer industry grew, so did the language.
Basic pioneered the interactive session. It offered <color=#3366CC>operating system</color> commands within its environment:
• The 'new' command created an empty slate.
• Statements evaluated immediately.
• Statements could be programmed by preceding them with line numbers.
• The 'list' command displayed the program.
• The 'run' command executed the program.
However, the Basic syntax was too simple for large programs. Recent dialects added structure and object-oriented
extensions. <color=#3366CC>Microsoft</color>'s Visual Basic is still widely used and produces a <color=#3366CC>graphical user interface</color>.
C
<color=#3366CC>C programming language</color> (1973) got its name because the language BCPL was replaced with B, and <color=#3366CC>AT&T Bell Labs</color>
called the next version "C". Its purpose was to write the <color=#3366CC>UNIX</color> <color=#3366CC>operating system</color>. C is a relatively small language,
making it easy to write compilers. Its growth mirrored the hardware growth in the 1980s. Its growth also was because it
has the facilities of <color=#3366CC>assembly language</color>, but it uses a <color=#3366CC>high-level syntax</color>. It added advanced features like:
• inline assembler
• arithmetic on pointers
• pointers to functions
• bit operations
• freely combining complex operators
C allows the programmer to control which region of memory data is to be stored. Global variables and static variables
require the fewest <color=#3366CC>clock cycles</color> to store. The stack is automatically used for the standard variable declarations. Heap
memory is returned to a <color=#3366CC>pointer variable</color> from the malloc function.
• The global and static data region is located just above the program region. (The program region is technically
called the text region. It is where machine instructions are stored.)
* The global and static data region is technically two regions. One region is called the initialized data segment, where
variables declared with default values are stored. The other region is called the block started by segment, where
variables declared without default values are stored. * Variables stored in the global and static data region have their
addresses set at compile time. They retain their values throughout the life of the process.
* The global and static region stores the global variables that are declared on top of (outside) the main function. Global
variables are visible to main and every other function in the source code.
On the other hand, variable declarations inside of main, other functions, or within { } block delimiters are local variables.
Local variables also include <color=#3366CC>formal parameter</color> variables. Parameter variables are enclosed within the parenthesis of a
function definition. Parameters provide an interface to the function.
* Local variables declared using the static prefix are also stored in the global and static data region. Unlike global
variables, static variables are only visible within the function or block. Static variables always retain their value. An
example usage would be the following function:
• The stack region is a contiguous block of memory located near the top memory address. Variables placed in the
stack are populated from top to bottom. A stack pointer is a special-purpose <color=#3366CC>register</color> that keeps track of the last
memory address populated. Variables are placed into the stack via the assembly language PUSH instruction.
Therefore, the addresses of these variables are set during <color=#3366CC>runtime</color>. The method for stack variables to lose their
scope is via the POP instruction.
* Local variables declared without the static prefix, including formal parameter variables, are called automatic variables
and are stored in the stack. They are visible inside the function or block and lose their scope upon exiting the function
or block.
• The heap region is located below the stack. It is populated from the bottom to the top. The <color=#3366CC>operating system</color>
manages the heap using a heap pointer and a list of allocated memory blocks. Like the stack, the addresses of
heap variables are set during runtime. An out of memory error occurs when the heap pointer and the stack pointer
meet.
* C provides the malloc library function to allocate heap memory. Populating the heap with data is an additional copy
function. Variables stored in the heap are economically passed to functions using pointers. Without pointers, the entire
block of data would have to be passed to the function via the stack.
In the 1970s, <color=#3366CC>software engineers</color> needed language support to break large projects down into <color=#3366CC>modules</color>. One obvious
feature was to decompose large projects physically into separate <color=#3366CC>files</color>. A less obvious feature was to decompose large
projects logically into <color=#3366CC>abstract datatypes</color>. At the time, languages supported concrete (scalar) datatypes like <color=#3366CC>integer</color>
numbers, <color=#3366CC>floating-point</color> numbers, and strings of characters. Abstract datatypes are structures of concrete datatypes,
with a new name assigned. For example, a list of integers could be called IntegerList.
Classes
In object-oriented terminology, an abstract datatype is called a class. However, a class is only a definition; no memory
is allocated. When memory is allocated to a class and bound to an identifier, it is called an object.
<color=#3366CC>C++</color> (1985) was originally called "C with Classes". It was designed to expand <color=#3366CC>C</color>'s capabilities by adding the
object-oriented facilities of the language Simula. A C++ class <color=#3366CC>encapsulates</color> related data items with the functions that
manipulate them.
<color=#3366CC>Object-oriented imperative languages</color> developed by combining the need for classes and the need for safe <color=#3366CC>functional</color>
<color=#3366CC>programming</color>. A <color=#3366CC>function</color>, in an object-oriented language, is assigned to a class. An assigned function is then referred
to as a method, member function, or <color=#3366CC>operation</color>. Object-oriented programming is executing operations on objects.
Inheritance
C++ supports a syntax to model <color=#3366CC>subset/superset</color> relationships. In <color=#3366CC>set theory</color>, an <color=#3366CC>element</color> of a subset inherits all the
attributes contained in the superset. For example, a student is a person. Therefore, the set of students is a subset of
the set of persons. As a result, students inherit all the attributes common to all persons. Additionally, students have
unique attributes that other people do not have. C++ models subset/superset relationships using <color=#3366CC>inheritance</color>.
Namespaces
A C++ namespace provides context in case a name conflict occurs. Class names and function names may be
duplicated in other source code files or third-party libraries. To wrap class names and function names in a namespace
block, use the keyword namespace. The keyword is followed by an identifier, and the block is enclosed in parenthesis.
To instantiate a class or execute a function that is within a namespace, prepend the class or function name with the
namespace name followed by a double colon. For example, my_namespace::my_function. Alternatively, execute the
using directive followed by the namespace name. Then all the class and function names may be accessed without the
double colon prefix.
Modules
A C++ module provides an improvement over the legacy #include preprocessor directive. The #include directive allows
for arbitrary files to be included in a C/C++ program. The goal is to have a common set of constants, datatypes, and
function declarations across a large application.
Modules are identified to the compiler by including the export module statement followed by the name of the module.
Other source code files then import the same module name to perform the module's task.
Class definitions and other named declarations must also be preceded with the export statement to be visible to other
source code files. If a namespace is exported, then everything inside that namespace is also exported.

Imperative languages have one major criticism: assigning an expression to a non-local variable may produce an
unintended side effect. <color=#3366CC>Declarative languages</color> generally omit the assignment statement and the control flow. They
describe what computation should be performed and not how to compute it. Two broad categories of declarative
languages are <color=#3366CC>functional languages</color> and <color=#3366CC>logical languages</color>.
The principle behind a functional language is to use <color=#3366CC>lambda calculus</color> as a guide for a well defined semantic. In
mathematics, a function is a rule that maps elements from an expression to a range of values. Consider the function:
times_10(x) = 10 * x
The expression 10 * x is mapped by the function times_10 to a range of values. One value happens to be 20. This
occurs when x is 2. So, the application of the function is mathematically written as:

stack before setting the program counter back to the calling function. The calling function will then pop the value from
the stack.
Imperative languages do support functions. Therefore, functional programming can be achieved in an imperative
language, if the programmer uses discipline. However, a functional language will force this discipline onto the
programmer through its syntax. Functional languages have a syntax tailored to emphasize the what.

Functional languages are used in <color=#3366CC>computer science</color> research to explore new language features. Moreover, their lack of
side-effects have made them popular in <color=#3366CC>parallel programming</color> and <color=#3366CC>concurrent programming</color>. However, application
developers prefer the <color=#3366CC>object-oriented features</color> of imperative languages.
Lisp
<color=#3366CC>Lisp</color> (1958) stands for "LISt Processor". It is tailored to process lists. A full structure of the data is formed by building
lists of lists. In memory, a <color=#3366CC>tree data structure</color> is built. Internally, the tree structure lends nicely for <color=#3366CC>recursive</color> functions.
The syntax to build a tree is to enclose the space-separated <color=#3366CC>elements</color> within parenthesis. The following is a <color=#3366CC>list</color> of three
elements. The first two elements are themselves lists of two elements:
((A B) (HELLO WORLD) 94)
Lisp has functions to extract and reconstruct elements. The function head returns a list containing the first element in
the list. The function tail returns a list containing everything but the first element. The function cons returns a list that is
the concatenation of other lists. Therefore, the following expression will return the list x:
cons(head(x), tail(x))
One drawback of Lisp is when many functions are nested, the parentheses may look confusing. Modern Lisp
<color=#3366CC>environments</color> help ensure parenthesis match. As an aside, Lisp does support the imperative language operations of
the assignment statement and goto loops. Also, Lisp is not concerned with the <color=#3366CC>datatype</color> of the elements at compile
time. Instead, it assigns (and may reassign) the datatypes at <color=#3366CC>runtime</color>. Assigning the datatype at runtime is called
dynamic binding. Whereas dynamic binding increases the language's flexibility, programming errors may linger until
late in the software development process.
Writing large, reliable, and readable Lisp programs requires forethought. If properly planned, the program may be much
shorter than an equivalent imperative language program. Lisp is widely used in <color=#3366CC>artificial intelligence</color>. However, its usage
has been accepted only because it has imperative language operations, making unintended side-effects possible.

Object-oriented programming
<color=#3366CC>Object-oriented programming</color> is a programming method to execute operations (<color=#3366CC>functions</color>) on objects. The basic idea is
to group the characteristics of a <color=#3366CC>phenomenon</color> into an object container and give the container a name. The operations
on the phenomenon are also grouped into the container. Object-oriented programming developed by combining the
need for containers and the need for safe <color=#3366CC>functional programming</color>. This programming method need not be confined to
an object-oriented language. In an object-oriented language, an object container is called a class. In a
non-object-oriented language, a <color=#3366CC>data structure</color> (which is also known as a record) may become an object container. To

structure is called an <color=#3366CC>abstract datatype</color>. However, <color=#3366CC>inheritance</color> will be missing. Nonetheless, this shortcoming can be
overcome.

Syntax and semantics
The <color=#3366CC>syntax</color> of a computer program is a <color=#3366CC>list</color> of production rules which form its <color=#3366CC>grammar</color>. A programming language's
grammar correctly places its declarations, expressions, and statements. Complementing the syntax of a language are
its semantics. The semantics describe the meanings attached to various syntactic constructs. A syntactic construct may
need a semantic description because a production rule may have an invalid interpretation. Also, different languages
might have the same syntax; however, their behaviors may be different.
The syntax of a language is formally described by listing the production rules. Whereas the syntax of a <color=#3366CC>natural</color>
<color=#3366CC>language</color> is extremely complicated, a subset of the English language can have this production rule listing:
• a sentence is made up of a noun-phrase followed by a verb-phrase;
• a noun-phrase is made up of an article followed by an adjective followed by a noun;
• a verb-phrase is made up of a verb followed by a noun-phrase;
• an article is 'the';
• an adjective is 'big' or
• an adjective is 'small';
• a noun is 'cat' or
• a noun is 'mouse';
• a verb is 'eats';
The words in bold-face are known as non-terminals. The words in 'single quotes' are known as terminals.
From this production rule listing, complete sentences may be formed using a series of replacements. The process is to
replace non-terminals with either a valid non-terminal or a valid terminal. The replacement process repeats until only
terminals remain. One valid sentence is:
• sentence
• noun-phrase verb-phrase
• article adjective noun verb-phrase
• the adjective noun verb-phrase
• the big noun verb-phrase
• the big cat verb-phrase
• the big cat verb noun-phrase
• the big cat eats noun-phrase
• the big cat eats article adjective noun
• the big cat eats the adjective noun
• the big cat eats the small noun
• the big cat eats the small mouse
However, another combination results in an invalid sentence:
• the small mouse eats the big cat
Therefore, a semantic is necessary to correctly describe the meaning of an eat activity.
One production rule listing method is called the <color=#3366CC>Backus–Naur form</color> (BNF). BNF describes the syntax of a language and
itself has a syntax. This recursive definition is an example of a metalanguage. The syntax of BNF includes:
• = which translates to is made up of a[n] when a non-terminal is to its right. It translates to is when a terminal is to its
right.
• | which translates to or.
• ‹ and › which surround non-terminals.
